items.stem: You changed a production prompt. What is the most reliable way to judge whether it improved?

options.text: Compare old and new versions on a labelled evaluation set with defined criteria
options.rationale: Correct: a labelled set with criteria gives a comparable, repeatable measure.

options.text: Try a couple of examples by hand and trust your impression
options.rationale: Anecdotal spot checks are not reliable evidence.

options.text: Ship it and wait for complaints
Pick whichever version has the longer prompt
options.rationale: Prompt length is not a quality measure.

items.explanation: Correct: a labelled set with criteria gives a comparable, repeatable measure.

items.stem: Which TWO practices support safe prompt changes over time? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Version each prompt with its rationale and evaluation scores
options.rationale: Correct: versioning with evidence makes changes auditable and reversible.

options.text: Run a regression set before each change ships
options.rationale: Correct: regression tests catch drift from an edit.

options.text: Edit the live prompt directly with no record
options.rationale: In-place edits lose history and auditability.

options.text: Optimise only a single metric and ignore the rest
options.rationale: A single-metric focus can hide regressions elsewhere.

items.explanation: Correct: versioning with evidence makes changes auditable and reversible.

items.stem: A prompt edit improves accuracy on one metric. Why is that not enough to ship it?

options.text: It may have regressed other behaviours; a regression set across metrics is needed
options.rationale: Correct: gains on one metric can mask losses on others.

options.text: One improved metric proves the change is strictly better
options.rationale: A single metric does not capture all behaviours.

options.text: Regression testing is unnecessary once accuracy rises
options.rationale: Regression testing guards exactly against such trade-offs.

options.text: Other metrics never change when one improves
options.rationale: Metrics frequently trade off against each other.

items.explanation: Correct: gains on one metric can mask losses on others.
